Pulp and Paper Industry Event 5 May 2011 Sanomatalo, Helsinki Liisa Rohweder Opening Words Your honorable minister Pema Gyamtsho, and Ambassador Sonam Tobden Rabgye other Himalayan guests, ladies and gentleman. I am very glad to see all of you here in our Pulp and Paper industry event. Please feel mostly welcome! This year WWF celebrates its 50th anniversary. However, this year is not only a year of celebration, but it will also mean us hard work together with many partners. Now, it is time for us in WWF to look backwards and also to analyze how we are moving towards our ambitious vision, which is a world where people live in harmony with nature. During the past 50 years WWF has helped to protect many of the planet´s most remarkable species and places and we have worked hard for slowing the growth of humanity´s ecological footprint. However, although we can witness many success stories, we are not yet on a sustainable pathway. Last year we published new information about the health of the world´s biodiversity and about humanity´s the ecological and water footprint. All these indicators clearly demonstrate that the drive for wealth and wellbeing of the past decades is putting unsustainable pressures on our planet. At the moment we consume natural resources of 1.5 planets yearly. In OECD countries even 3 planets yearly. If we all lived like US residents – 4.5 planets would be needed. Much of this is due to consumption in highly developed countries ‐ Average American consumes equivalent of 43 Africans. The increase in the ecological footprint has had an impact on the biodiversity. WWF measures the level of biodiversity with the living planet index. And the living planet index, which concretizes the level of biodiversity has decreased by 30 per cent since 1970. Rapid economic growth in the highly developed countries has caused an ever‐growing demand for resources – for food and drink, energy, transport, electronic products, living space, and space to dispose our waste, particularly carbon dioxide.

As the resources for our production and consumption can no longer be sourced from highly developed countries, they are increasingly imported from developing countries. Only about 20 % of the world’s people live in the OECD, but we account for almost 40 % of ecological footprint. The implications are clear. The Living Planet index shows that the biodiversity has decreased in the tropical areas, that is, in the world´s poorest countries, by 60 % since 1970. As an example of the biodiversity decrease I give you tropical forest loss. Forests are cleared every year with an area the size of Greece, or almost the size of Nepal. This means that the business as usual and the way we live is not an option. We must find ways to live much more lightly on the earth. We need to take better care about nature and its ecosystem services not only for our survival but also for global responsibility and for the nature itself, for its own value. What is positive, is that private sector is increasing its engagement in conservation. Leading global businesses are taking significant steps to reduce their ecological footprint. The market for responsibly sourced wood, paper, seafood, palm oil and other commodities is growing. Thus, there is space for optimism and we have the possibility to reach our ambitious goaI which is that by 2020 biodiversity is protected and well managed in the world’s most outstanding natural places and ecological footprint has started to decrease. However, radical changes in the way we live, and produce goods and services, need to happen urgently. We did not succeed during the past 50 years. We cannot afford to wait for another 50 years. This event is part of the solution and progress towards our ambitious goals. It is important to understand, that we do not want to tell you what should be done in our mind but we want to find the solutions together and of course commit all of you behind them. Today we focus on pulp and paper industry´s role in creating a “one‐planet” economy and we focus on plantations. Much plantation expansion in Latin America, Asia and Africa to date has come from the conversation of natural forests and other high conservation value areas such as wetlands. In many cases, their establishment has also had significant social consequences due to ignoring the rights and interests of local communities.

However, well managed plantations can be compatible with both biodiversity conservation and human needs. We all know that plantations can never provide the same range of biodiversity as natural forests. Still, in cases where land has been used in an unsustainable way such as overgrazing, they may help to recover some ecosystem services and biodiversity. A central question today is: How we can save the forests and supply the people of the world with all the fibre and paper products they need remembering that we are now 6.7 billion and in 2050 9.2 billion. We have a challenging objective, but it is not impossible. It contributes partly to WWF’s goal of ending the biodiversity loss by 2020. As to the forests this goal means end to the deforestation and forest degradation by 2020. We can achieve this goal if we feel it is important and we have the will. However, its important to understand that there is no time to waste. Business as usual is no more an option. I am optimistic, because with you and with many other stakeholders we can find solutions and make a change to happen. At the end I would like to thank Lenzing Papier, Metso, Metsähallitus, Metsäliitto,Nokia and UPM for supporting this event and WWF Finland´s year of the forest. As part of the WWF global Living forest Campaign, our focus is on deforestation of tropical forests and on biodiversity of Finnish forests. These companies do not only support our work financially but they also support our goals by making changes happen in their own businesses. Sanomatalo I would like to thank for hosting the seminar. Finally I wish you all a fruitful event and innovative thoughts!
